summary.value: The authors introduce AR3PO, a sampling-efficient RLVR method that fixes GRPO’s vanishing advantage problem, where all responses in a group get identical rewards and yield zero gradient, by combining two ideas: adaptive rollout and response reuse. Adaptive rollout allocates more generations to hard prompts in staged rounds while saving compute on easy ones, and response reuse supplies training signal by leveraging previously generated correct answers with careful handling. Multiple experiment results over different benchmarks is presented, benchmarking against previous methods DAPO and original GRPO.

strengths.value:
- The paper tries to tackle an important aspect of RLVR vanishing gradient obstacle, which is timely
- Experiments are conducted over multiple sets of model families (Qwen/Llama)
- The motivation is clear for building a sampling-efficient method

weaknesses.value:
**[w1] The experiment setup and presentation is unclear and problematic:**
- Please report the baseline performance before training, this is necessary to assess the training improvement.
- Improvement is very marginal (<1pp) when comparing to GRPO, which has the relatively similar response sampling efficiency.
-  I am concerned that whether the baseline results are replicated in its actual performance, as the full experiment setup is different from DAPO paper. Given only single-run results are reported, and the credibility of the result is less persuasive. Please consider to report avg & std running results across multiple runs of the baselines along with your methods to increase credibility of your results.
- Also, the training curve for actual accuracy, e.g., the one for the validation set, only includes your method. I would suggest to plot the validation curve for the other method as well along with yours to provide a direct comparison, which could greatly strengthen the credibility and effectiveness of your method. 
- You are working on 32B model, but why not disclose the result in Table 1?

**[w2] clarity should be improved; some explanation and presentation read confusing**
- For the result in Figure 3, it reads very surprising, as DAPO requires 2000 steps while yours only need 130 steps. Such surprising results would also confuse readers and raise the concern regarding training setup, as in the previous experiment, the difference between yours and DAPO is very minor. **Also, in DAPO paper, at around 100 steps, avg@32 on AIME24 is only around 5%, but in your Figure 3, it reaches 15% even for the first validation point; this raises strong concerns regarding the evaluation protocols**. To improve clarity, please include the DAPO results trained using your setup and plot the curve till 150 steps. This is the best way to consolidate this surprising result.
- Check Q1-Q3 in question sections, please clarify. 
- Sampling numbers wouldn't fully reflect the training time; I suggest to include the actual training time for methods in table 1 to better highlight your training efficiency.

questions.value:
- For adaptive rollout, I cannot see any technique difference between yours and DAPO, as both will stop sampling until one correct response is sampled out. The only difference I see is that you will remove these response from the prompt space, while DAPO won't. Also, DAPO can also be treated as an "adaptive weighting" as they will also spend more rollouts over the difficult questions. 
- I still don't understand how the response reuse could resolve the problem of all-negative-sample group. The reuse technique is based on the assumption that the prompt has been resolved, which is a minor case for the problem I believe; for unsolved problems, it has no correct response to use.
- Para from line 216 to line 222 reads confusing, please consider to re-write it to make it clear.

comment.value: We apologize for not making it clear enough in our manuscript. In Section 4.5, when we state that we follow the setup in Yu et al. (2025), we mean that we use a PPO mini-batch size of 32, which results in 16 gradient updates per step (since 512 / 32 = 16), the same as DAPO. Under this setting, our step 130 corresponds to roughly 2000 gradient updates in their figure. We will make it clearer in the next version.

**Table 1: it is hard to assess whether AR3PO’s performance differences are statistically significant compared to the two other methods compared against.**

Due to the high computational cost of LLM-based RLVR training, it is very common in recent RLVR papers that variance or confidence intervals are not reported, especially when using large models. We want to emphasize that our experiments cover **7B, 8B, and 32B** models across two different base model families, demonstrating the **scalability** of our method across different model sizes. Our method consistently achieves performance comparable to DAPO, one of the strongest RLVR baselines, while reducing the generation cost by up to **4.2×**.

**Baseline methods for comparison yield a somewhat limited empirical assessment of performance.**

We would like to point out that, at the time of conducting this project, DAPO was already one of the strongest RLVR baselines, and comparing against DAPO and GRPO is also standard practice in recent RLVR papers. Thus, our choice of baselines aligns with the common evaluation protocol in the field. From the experiments, our method achieves a 4.2× reduction in rollout cost while maintaining performance comparable to DAPO. Given that DAPO itself is a strong baseline, obtaining similar performance with significantly lower rollout cost demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

**The two models used are of similar capacity (7B vs 8B params). It would be useful to know how this method performs on a smaller and much larger model.**

We want to clarify again that our experiments cover **7B, 8B, and 32B** models across two different base model families, demonstrating the **scalability** of our method across a range of model sizes. Since LLM research typically emphasizes scalability rather than small-model behavior, and we already include experiments up to **32B**, we believe that conducting additional experiments on smaller models would not provide meaningful insights for validating our claims.

**Did you assess the three methods on pass@X for any of the benchmark tasks? While for lower X, this is a noisier, higher variance metric, it would be interesting to know how the methods compare in terms of yielding more diverse rollouts.**

We follow the standard evaluation protocol in RLVR, which reports the average performance over 8 rollouts (for large datasets) or 64 rollouts (for small datasets). According to previous research, post-training methods primarily aim to increase the probability of generating correct responses. Therefore, average@X is generally a more stable and meaningful metric for evaluating RLVR performance.

**For transparency, can you please provide a breakdown of the resulting benchmark task makeup, including number of examples, after you apply the filtering?**

We only apply filtering to the training set DAPO-Math, and as stated in lines 267–268, we remove the non-English prompts and 14K prompts remain after filtering. There is no filtering applied to the evaluation benchmarks.

**Why did you only evaluate Qwen2.5-7B as the base model in Table 2, instead of also evaluating Llama-3.1-8B?**

Due to limited computational resources and project time constraints, we conducted the detailed study of different reuse strategies primarily on Qwen2.5-7B. Our results show that the proposed response reuse techniques achieve a clear performance advantage over the direct rollout replay strategies used in previous works.

summary.value:
This paper addresses the rollout costs of using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) in the context of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). The work presents a two-pronged approach to improving sample efficiency in RLVR with:
* Adaptive rollout: dynamically allocates more responses to “difficult prompts” than easier ones
* Response reuse: uses previously generated correct responses as training signals
Empirical evaluation of the methods centers on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen and Llama base models, showing comparable or better performance compared to GRPO and DAPO baselines while improving rollout costs.

strengths.value:
* Motivation for the two complementary ideas suggested by the authors—adaptive rollout and response reuse—are motivated by “GRPO’s potential inefficiency” (l 74). 
* Algorithm presentation is simple and straightforward. Direct comparison of the difference between AR3PO and GRPO creates an easy-to-follow illustration of the extension of the author’s proposed approach (Sec 3.2).
* The paper seems promising, with a clear method and potentially promising initial empirical evaluation, though the reviewer believes broader, more thorough empirical substantiation is required (refer to Weaknesses section).

weaknesses.value:
* Table 1: it is hard to assess whether AR3PO’s performance differences are statistically significant compared to the two other methods compared against. Are these metrics across a single run of the algorithm? Can you provide error bars for these results? Additionally, these would be useful in Table 2. 
* Baseline methods for comparison yield a somewhat limited empirical assessment of performance. While the two methods that are compared against are appropriate choices—vanilla GRPO, which the proposed method is an extension of, and DAPO, a recent method with dynamic sampling strategy—additional points of comparison would help create a more convincing story of the performance benefits the authors claim AR3PO provides. 
* The two models used are of similar capacity (7B vs 8B params). It would be useful to know how this method performs on a smaller and much larger model.

summary.value: This paper proposes AR3PO, a novel RLVR framework for improving post-training efficiency in large language models (LLMs). Existing RL-for-reasoning methods rely on fixed rollout budgets and discard previously correct responses, thus they have severe sampling inefficiency issues and advantage vanishing problems. This work introduces a rollout strategy that dynamically allocates sampling resources with historically correct outputs. It mainly contains  1) an adaptive scheduler, to assign more rollouts to harder prompts based on difficulty estimation, 2) a response reuse mechanism, to maintain effective gradient signals under uniform reward conditions. The authors provide experimental results to show that AR3PO effectively prevents advantage vanishing and significantly reduces sampling cost.

strengths.value:
The motivation of improving sampling efficiency is reasonable. Most existing work focuses on fixed-budget RL for reasoning, but these approaches cannot handle prompt-specific difficulty or reuse prior correct responses. This would limit training efficiency and stability. This paper dynamically allocates rollouts and reuses verified correct samples, which improves gradient utilization and reduces cost in RLVR.

The workflow is well-structured. This approach balances computational allocation across tasks and further stabilizes policy optimization by mitigating the advantage vanishing issue.

Open code. Most of the information is included.

weaknesses.value:
According to the descriptions, this AR3PO relies heavily on difficulty estimation and response caching during rollout process. This brings additional implementation complexity and even instability if the difficulty metric is poorly calibrated. There is no discussion (or limitation part) of this extra computational overhead. The trade-off between the computational cost and efficiency gains is a very important problem in RL for reasoning, which should not be avoided.

The baselines are limited. The paper only compares with GRPO and DAPO. Adding other efficient RL baselines would make the results more convincing, as this paper is not the first one targeting efficiency issues.

The experimental design is not complete. 1) No ablation study to isolate the individual contributions of each component; 2) The experiments are conducted on only two models, without statistical measures such as variance or confidence intervals.

questions.value: See above. And the authors may consider using Qwen 2.5's 1.5B or Qwen 3's smaller models for more results. For me, the 7b and 8b models are almost the same size, and adding a time report would strengthen the claims.

comment.value:
We respond to the weaknesses and questions below.

**This brings additional implementation complexity and even instability if the difficulty metric is poorly calibrated. There is no discussion (or limitation part) of this extra computational overhead.**

We would like to clarify several misunderstandings in this comment.

First, any newly proposed RLVR algorithm inevitably introduces some implementation complexity, and this is not specific to our method. More importantly, this implementation detail has nothing to do with computational overhead, and we believe conflating the two is inaccurate.

Second, our setting follows the standard RLVR framework where a verifier evaluates the correctness of generated responses. Under this setup, we are unsure why the reviewer believes the difficulty metric would be “poorly calibrated,” or why this would induce instability. 

Third, the claim about “extra computational overhead” does not match what our method actually does. Our adaptive rollout strategy **reduces generation cost** and significantly lowers the number of sampled trajectories. Meanwhile, the response reuse mechanism simply replaces incorrect responses with previously generated correct ones, and therefore **does not introduce any additional computational overhead**. Both components are explicitly designed to improve efficiency rather than increase cost.

**The baselines are limited.**

We would like to point out that, at the time of conducting this project, DAPO was already one of the strongest RLVR baselines, and comparing against DAPO and GRPO is also standard practice in recent RLVR papers. Thus, our choice of baselines aligns with the common evaluation protocol in the field.
As emphasized throughout the paper, our primary goal is to **improve the sampling efficiency** of RLVR algorithms. In this regard, our method achieves a **4.2× reduction in rollout cost** while maintaining performance comparable to DAPO. Given that DAPO itself is a strong baseline, obtaining similar performance with significantly lower rollout cost demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

**The experiments are conducted on only two models, without statistical measures such as variance or confidence intervals.**

We conduct experiments using two different base models from two distinct model families to verify the effectiveness and generality of our method. Due to the high computational cost of LLM-based RLVR training, it is very common in recent RLVR papers that variance or confidence intervals are not reported, especially when using large models.
Our experiments cover **7B, 8B, and 32B** models, demonstrating the **scalability** of our method across different model sizes. Since LLM research typically emphasizes scalability rather than small-model behavior, and we already include experiments up to **32B**, we believe conducting additional experiments on very small models (e.g., 1.5B) would not provide meaningful insights for validating our claims.

We respond to the weaknesses and questions below.

**Limited novelty. The algorithmic design is standard and common practice. The main change is to adjust rollout allocation adaptively and reuse previous correct responses. Beyond this incremental modification, the method does not introduce a new learning paradigm.**

We would like to clarify that our paper proposes a novel RLVR algorithm that introduces **two new techniques**: adaptive rollout for trajectory sampling and response reuse for replaying previously generated valid trajectories. In Section 5, we have clearly stated the differences between our method and other related or concurrent works, and these distinctions go beyond what we would consider incremental changes.

Regarding the comment on a “new learning paradigm,” we are not entirely sure what this refers to. All recent RLVR works are based on policy-gradient methods and follow the general GRPO pipeline. If the definition of “novelty” is tied strictly to creating an entirely new paradigm, then by this standard none of the recent RLVR works would qualify as novel, which we believe would be an unfair criterion. Therefore, we argue that our contributions are meaningful and sufficiently novel.

**The model comparisons are relatively narrow. The proposed AR3PO shows efficiency gains, whereas its performance advantage is marginal over DAPO. Without broader benchmarks or stronger baselines, the claimed improvements are hard to fully justify.**

We would like to point out that, at the time of conducting this project, DAPO was already one of the strongest RLVR baselines, and comparing against DAPO and GRPO is also standard practice in recent RLVR papers. Thus, our choice of baselines aligns with the common evaluation protocol in the field.

As emphasized throughout the paper, our primary goal is to **improve the sampling efficiency** of RLVR algorithms. In this regard, our method achieves a **4.2× reduction in rollout cost** while maintaining performance comparable to DAPO. Given that DAPO itself is a strong baseline, obtaining similar performance with significantly lower rollout cost demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

**Authors did not conduct comprehensive ablation studies for the proposed method.**

We would like to clarify that we did conduct ablation studies for the key components of our method. In Figure 1, we compare our adaptive rollout strategy with the dynamic sampling strategy used in DAPO, showing that our method reduces generation cost by approximately 4.2×. In Section 4.3, we further compare our proposed response reuse technique with the direct rollout replay used in other works, and our method achieves a clear performance advantage. These ablations isolate the contributions of both proposed components and demonstrate their effectiveness.

**Including mcode generation or logical QA tasks would help.**

In this paper, we focus our experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks, as they are representative in RLVR. However, our algorithm is not limited to this domain and can be readily extended to other tasks such as code generation or logical QA. We agree that exploring these directions would be valuable, and we consider them as future work.

**How sensitive is AR3PO to the choice of hyperparameters, eg number of rollout stages?**

In this paper, we focus on improving the sampling efficiency of RLVR algorithms and adopt a 2-stage rollout design to balance the tradeoff between performance and efficiency. Based on our experimental observations, the performance continues to increase when more rollout stages are used. Therefore, our method is generally robust under different choices, with additional stages providing further gains at the cost of increased rollout.

summary.value: This paper proposes a method to improve sampling efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) through AR3PO. The authors specifically compared AR3PO with GRPO and DAPO on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen and Llama base models. They provide results showing that AR3PO achieves comparable or better accuracy than DAPO while reducing rollout cost.

2. The motivation and the method proposed in this paper are easy to understand.

3. The idea of combining adaptive rollout and response reuse is intuitive and aligns well with the efficiency goal in RLVR training.

comment.value:
We believe the reviewer has several major **misunderstanding** of our algorithmic design and experimental results, and we will clarify each point in detail.

**For adaptive rollout, I cannot see any technique difference between yours and DAPO**

We want to clarify that our adaptive rollout and the dynamic sampling used in DAPO are two **completely different** rollout strategies. Our method divides the sampling process into multiple stages and keeps generating new responses only for prompts without correct responses. In contrast, DAPO oversamples the prompt set by 3×, then uniformly samples responses for these prompts and selects prompts with non-zero reward variance.
Although both approaches share the motivation of ensuring that prompts obtain correct responses, the actual rollout strategies are completely different. As a result, our algorithm significantly reduces the generation cost by **4.2×**. We are therefore not sure why the reviewer **cannot see any technique difference** between these two methods.

**I still don't understand how the response reuse could resolve the problem of all-negative-sample group.**

Our experimental results in Figure 2(c) **clearly** show that we reduce the zero-reward prompt ratio from 0.3 to 0.2, which is consistent with our observation that about 10% of prompts have reused responses during training. This directly demonstrates that response reuse helps mitigate the all-negative-sample issue by providing valid trajectories for prompts that would otherwise have no correct responses.
We have highlighted this observation in both the introduction and the experimental section, and the empirical evidence in Figure 2(c) supports the effectiveness of our approach. Therefore, we are not sure why the reviewer believes it is a minor case.

**I am concerned that whether the baseline results are replicated in its actual performance, as the full experiment setup is different from DAPO paper.**

In the caption of Figure 3, we **clearly** state that “DAPO’s figure reports gradient update steps, with 16 updates per step; thus, our step 130 approximately corresponds to their step 2000.” This directly addresses the difference in step definitions and aligns the curves on a comparable basis.
Moreover, our experimental setup for the 32B model **exactly** follows both the training configuration and the evaluation protocol used in the DAPO paper. There is no deviation in model choice, reward design, batch size, optimizer setup, or evaluation criteria. Given this, we do not see any substantive reason for the reviewer’s **strong concerns** about the correctness of our experimental setup, as the claim appears to arise from a **misunderstanding** of how step normalization is handled rather than from any actual discrepancy in methodology.

**Report avg & std running results**

We conduct experiments using two different base models from two distinct model families to verify the effectiveness and generality of our method. Due to the high computational cost of LLM-based RLVR training, it is very common in recent RLVR papers that variance or confidence intervals are not reported, especially when using large models.

**Improvement is marginal**

We want to emphasize that our method achieves performance comparable to DAPO while **reducing the generation cost by 4.2x**. More importantly, our algorithm provides a sampling-efficient solution to the vanishing advantage issue, rather than relying on the direct oversampling strategy used in DAPO.
